senses.definition: The English alphabet.
senses.example: Do you know your ABC? (US: Do you know your ABCs?)

senses.definition: The fundamentals of any subject.
senses.example: the ABC of finance

senses.definition: A straightforward, uniform playing style, often focusing on betting for value, folding weak hands, and avoiding bluffing.
senses.example: Her ABC style of poker kept her from bluffing and made her easy to read at the table.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of ABC store.
Initialism of airway, breathing and circulation, the essential steps in the immediate assessment and treatment of critically ill or injured patients.
senses.example: Paramedics checked his ABC first, making sure his airway was clear and his breathing was steady.

senses.definition: Initialism of alcoholic beverage control.
senses.example: The state ABC board suspended the bar's liquor license after repeated underage drinking violations.

senses.definition: Initialism of American-born Chinese.
senses.example: She grew up in Ohio as an ABC, speaking English at home and Cantonese only with her grandparents.

senses.definition: Initialism of Australian-born Chinese.
senses.example: Her cousin, an ABC from Sydney, visited San Francisco and loved the food in Chinatown.

senses.definition: Initialism of activity-based costing.
senses.example: Our finance team used ABC to allocate overhead costs to each product line more accurately.

senses.definition: Initialism of advance base camp.
senses.example: The expedition reached ABC at dawn, where the climbers rested before attempting the summit push.

senses.definition: Initialism of ATP-binding cassette.
senses.example: ABC transporter

senses.definition: Initialism of antigen-binding capacity.
senses.example: The lab measured the ABC of each antibody sample to compare their binding strength.

senses.definition: Initialism of age-associated B cell.
senses.example: Researchers found that ABC populations expanded in older patients with chronic autoimmune disease.

senses.definition: Initialism of aneurysmal bone cyst.
senses.example: The radiologist diagnosed an ABC in the patient's femur and recommended surgical curettage.

senses.definition: Initialism of adenoid basal cell carcinoma.
senses.example: Pathology confirmed the tumor was an ABC, a slow-growing skin cancer typically found on the face.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of abacavir.
senses.example: His doctor prescribed ABC along with lamivudine as part of his daily HIV treatment.

senses.definition: Initialism of accelerated blood clearance.
senses.example: Repeated doses of the nanoparticle triggered ABC, so the drug was cleared from circulation within hours.

senses.definition: Initialism of Atanasoff-Berry computer.
senses.example: The history class learned that the ABC was built in Iowa before ENIAC existed.

senses.definition: Initialism of artificial bee colony.
senses.example: We tuned the neural network's weights using ABC, an optimization algorithm inspired by foraging bees.

senses.definition: Initialism of assignment for the benefit of creditors.
senses.example: The struggling manufacturer made an ABC with its lenders, selling its assets to pay off its debts.

senses.definition: Initialism of absorbing boundary condition.
Initialism of abstract base class.
Initialism of adventure-based counseling.
Initialism of affect, behavior, and cognition.
Initialism of alien big cat.
Initialism of active body control.
Initialism of Archbishop of Canterbury.
A keyboard layout in which all keys are arranged in alphabetical order in English.
Initialism of atomic, biological and chemical, the three main categories of weapon of mass destruction.
Initialism of already been chewed.
Initialism of activated B-cell-like.
Initialism of anything but Chardonnay, a backlash against Chardonnay wine, seen as ubiquitous.
Initialism of abstinence, be faithful, use a condom, a sex education policy developed in response to the epidemic of HIV/AIDS in Africa.
Initialism of always be charging, a recommendation to remember to charge or be left without use by a low battery at an inopportune time.
Initialism of anything but Conservative.

core.definition: The English alphabet, or the basic fundamentals of any subject.

pronunciation.tip: Say each letter separately, with the strongest stress on AY. In the plural form 'the ABCs', the final s sounds like z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. 'The ABCs of' a subject is a friendly way to say its basics, and it carries no negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the ABCs for the alphabet, especially the alphabet song kids learn in preschool. 'The ABCs of' something, as in 'the ABCs of investing,' means the essentials, and it sounds friendly rather than condescending. A natural reply is to just ask for the next step, since the phrase is often a starting point.

distinctions.note: Alphabet is the formal, general word for the full set of letters; ABC is the everyday, child-friendly name, often used for the song or for basics.
Basics is a neutral, general word for fundamentals; the ABCs suggests the most elementary foundation, often for a skill being learned from scratch.

examples.everyday: My daughter just learned her ABCs, and she sings them in the car every morning.
examples.professional: Before the new analysts join, I walk them through the ABCs of our data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Any serious account of early literacy has to begin with the ABCs of how children map letters onto sounds.

nuance.analogy: Like training wheels on a bicycle, the ABCs are the simple support you build everything else on.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the names of the first three letters of the alphabet, A, B and C.
common_mistakes: Saying it as one word, like 'ab-see'; the letters are pronounced separately.
Using it as a countable noun without 'the' in a general sense; say 'the alphabet' or 'the ABCs' rather than 'an ABC' for the whole system.

abc.etymology: From Middle English *abece*, *ABC*, from the first three letters of the Latin alphabet, standing for the whole alphabet.

core.definition: A common Hebrew name in the Bible, borne by several people, including a king of Judah, the son of the prophet Samuel, and a priest whose course is named in Luke.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BY. The final syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the 'j' sound is a soft 'dj' like in 'jam'. Do not pronounce the final h.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name, so Americans use it only when referring to a specific biblical person. In church settings, people might mention the priestly course of Abijah or the king of Judah. Note that Abijah appears in Chronicles while the same king appears as Abijam in Kings.

examples.everyday: Abijah is a name I hear in Bible study, and it's a lot easier to say than some others.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan, I noted that Abijah is both a king of Judah and a priestly course in 1 Chronicles 24.
examples.analytical: The Chronicler's presentation of Abijah as a victorious king in 2 Chronicles 13 differs sharply from the portrayal of his reign in 1 Kings.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Avijah', meaning 'Yah is my father' or 'my father is Yah'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the king Abijah in Chronicles with Abijam in Kings, which are two names for the same king.
Saying 'uh-BY-jah' with a hard 'j', when the American pronunciation has a soft 'j' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: Abijah (Hebrew Avijah, 'Yah is my father') is borne by several people in the Old Testament. 1 Samuel 8:2 names a son of Samuel who, with his brother, took bribes as a judge in Beersheba. 2 Chronicles 13 describes King Abijah of Judah, son of Rehoboam, who defeated Jeroboam of Israel in battle. 1 Chronicles 24:10 lists the eighth priestly course as belonging to Abijah, and Luke 1:5 notes that Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, was of that course.

senses.definition: Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loathsome; execrable.
senses.example: abominable crime

senses.definition: Very bad or inferior.
Disagreeable or unpleasant.
senses.example: abominable weather

core.definition: Extremely bad, unpleasant, or morally disgusting. Used for things that are hateful or very poor in quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the second syllable, BAH. The 'o' in the first syllable is the cot vowel (like 'father'), and the last syllable is a weak, almost silent 'bul'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. In everyday speech it is often used playfully or with exaggeration, as in 'abominable weather'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'abominable' in both serious and casual ways. In casual talk, you might say 'The traffic was abominable' to complain without sounding harsh. For serious moral judgments, it sounds formal and strong, so use it carefully in personal conversation to avoid sounding overly dramatic.

distinctions.note: Terrible is a common everyday word for bad things; abominable is stronger and more formal, suggesting disgust.
Awful is casual and widely used; abominable suggests a more intense or moral sense of disgust.

examples.everyday: The weather this weekend was abominable, so we stayed inside and watched movies.
examples.professional: The vendor's support response times were abominable, so we moved the contract to another provider.
examples.analytical: The author describes the regime's treatment of prisoners as abominable, insisting that no political goal can justify such cruelty.

nuance.analogy: Something abominable is like a rotten smell in a room: you want to get away from it as quickly as possible.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abominari, meaning 'to deprecate as an ill omen', from ab- (away) and omen.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'uh-MIN-uh-bul' and stressing the wrong part of the word.
Using 'abominable' for mild dislike; it is too strong for ordinary disappointments.

abominable.etymology: From Middle English *abhomynable*, from Old French *abominable*, from Late Latin *abōminābilis* (“deserving abhorrence”), from *abōminor* (“abhor, deprecate as an ill omen”), from *ab* (“, away from”) + *ōminor* (“forebode, predict, presage”), from *ōmen*…

core.definition: God's promise to Abraham of land, descendants and blessing for all nations, marked by circumcision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HAM in Abrahamic, and on KUV in covenant. The first part is 'ay-bruh,' with a weak middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly; positive in religious contexts for its promise of blessing.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theology, Bible study and religious studies. Americans in church may say "God's promise to Abraham." Do not confuse it with the phrase Abrahamic religions (Judaism, Christianity, Islam).

distinctions.note: The Mosaic covenant is the law given at Sinai through Moses, centuries after Abraham.
The Davidic covenant promises David an enduring dynasty.
The new covenant, promised by Jeremiah and taught in the New Testament, is fulfilled in Christ.

examples.everyday: Our pastor said the Abrahamic covenant is the starting point for the whole story of Israel.
examples.professional: Tonight's Bible study is on the Abrahamic covenant in Genesis 12 and 15.
examples.analytical: Paul argues in Galatians 3 that the Abrahamic covenant, grounded in promise, precedes and is not annulled by the law.

nuance.analogy: The root of a tree: later covenants grow from the promise made to Abraham.
nuance.etymology: Abrahamic from Abraham (Hebrew Avraham, probably "father of a multitude"); covenant from Latin convenire, to come together.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable (a-bra-HAM-ic with stress on ABR).
Confusing it with the Abrahamic religions.
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 12:1-3 God calls Abram to go to a new land and promises a great nation, a name and blessing for all families of the earth. Genesis 15 ratifies the covenant in a ritual in which God alone passes between the pieces, and Genesis 17 adds the sign of circumcision and renames him Abraham. Hebrew berit means covenant. Paul's reading is in Romans 4 and Galatians 3.

traditions.view: Many emphasize its fulfillment in Christ and the church as Abraham's spiritual offspring, while dispensationalists maintain a continuing role for national Israel. Baptists tie circumcision less to infant baptism than do Reformed paedobaptists.
Sees the covenant fulfilled in Christ and the Church, with circumcision prefiguring baptism, which is the sacrament of entry into the new covenant.
Sees Abraham as a model of faith and the promises fulfilled in Christ; circumcision is understood as a type of baptism.

senses.definition: One who abstains; especially, one who abstains from something, such as the use of alcohol or drugs, or one who abstains for religious reasons; one who practices self-denial.
senses.example: As a lifelong abstainer, my uncle has never touched a drop of alcohol.

core.definition: A person who deliberately chooses not to do something, especially not to drink alcohol, usually as a settled choice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STAY, the second syllable. The final -er is a reduced, r-colored schwa, so say 'ner' rather than 'nair'. Do not put the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound admirable (self-discipline) or distant, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: In casual talk, Americans usually say 'nondrinker', 'I don't drink', or 'teetotaler', and teetotaler can sound old-fashioned or teasing. The word 'abstainer' appears more in health, religious, and formal contexts, and in news about votes, where abstainers are members who choose not to vote yes or no.

distinctions.note: A teetotaler never drinks alcohol at all, often out of conviction; the word is informal and sometimes old-fashioned.
Abstinent is an adjective describing restraint or self-denial, while abstainer is the person who abstains.
Nondrinker is plain, neutral everyday English; abstainer sounds more deliberate or formal.

examples.everyday: I'm a lifelong abstainer, so just get me some sparkling water.
examples.professional: Eight members voted yes, two voted no, and the rest were abstainers, so the motion passed.
examples.analytical: Historically, the abstainer's refusal of wine was read as a witness to self-denial rather than as a legal rule.

nuance.analogy: Like a player who sits out a play on purpose instead of joining either side.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abstinere, 'to hold back,' from abs- 'away' and tenere 'to hold.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in AB-stayner; the stress belongs on STAY.
Using it for someone who is just not drinking tonight; the word suggests a settled, long-term choice.

senses.definition: Supplying with or obliging; accommodating.
senses.example: The company's accommodative policies made it easy for employees to request flexible schedules.

core.definition: Willing to adjust to others' needs, or (in economics) tending to ease conditions and support growth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAH, the cot vowel. The final -ive is a short 'iv' sound, not 'eev', and the -ative syllable is weak.

nuance.connotation: Positive for people and neutral for policy. In economics it describes measures that boost growth, not a moral quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use accommodative mainly in economic news and formal writing, as in 'accommodative monetary policy' from the Federal Reserve. For a person's kindness, say accommodating, which is much more common. In vision science, the word also describes the eye's focusing ability.

distinctions.note: Accommodating is the everyday word for a helpful person, while accommodative is more formal and often used for policies or technical systems.
Obliging means willing to do someone a favor, while accommodative means willing to adjust or make room for needs.

examples.everyday: My landlord has been pretty accommodative about letting us pay late this month.
examples.professional: The central bank's accommodative stance kept interest rates low through most of the recovery.
examples.analytical: A theology that is too accommodative to its culture may lose the prophetic edge that Scripture demands.

nuance.analogy: Like a camera lens that adjusts its focus to what the eye needs to see.
nuance.etymology: From accommodate, from Latin accommodare, plus the suffix -ive.
common_mistakes: Using accommodative for a person; the usual word is accommodating.
Confusing accommodative with accommodation, which is the noun meaning lodging or a settlement.

senses.definition: Doomed to destruction or misery; cursed; anathematized.
Hateful; detestable, loathsome.
senses.example: Grandma called the accursed tax form the worst thing ever invented by bureaucrats.

core.definition: Under a curse, doomed to destruction or misery; in everyday use, 'this accursed' means extremely annoying or hateful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KUR. The American 'er' vowel is rhotic and the ending is a short 'id', not 'ed', when used before a noun.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it is strong and dramatic, and used jokingly it signals frustration.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech it appears mostly in a joking way, as in 'this accursed printer,' to express exasperation. In serious contexts it means truly doomed or cursed, and it is common in literature and Bible-related talk. Using it before a noun is typical; 'cursed' is more common in ordinary speech.

distinctions.note: Cursed is the everyday word and works in most contexts; accursed is more emphatic and literary, usually placed before a noun.
Damned is a stronger word that can be a swear word in casual speech; accursed is more formal and less offensive.

examples.everyday: This accursed Wi-Fi keeps dropping right when I'm on a call.
examples.professional: That accursed deployment script failed again in production, and we still don't know why.
examples.analytical: Paul wishes himself accursed for the sake of his kinsmen in Romans 9:3, a striking reversal of the devoted thing.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note that won't come off: the bad luck clings to the thing and won't let go.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English acursen, from Old English ācursian, to curse thoroughly, with the intensifying prefix a-.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final ed as /ɛd/ instead of /ɪd/ when it is an adjective.
Using 'accursed' in very casual speech where 'cursed' or 'annoying' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'accused', which means charged with a crime.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament the idea is expressed by the Hebrew herem, something devoted to God and therefore set apart for destruction (Joshua 6:17). In Galatians 1:8-9 Paul uses the Greek anathema, meaning 'let him be accursed,' for those who preach a different gospel. Romans 9:3 shows Paul wishing he could be accursed for the sake of his fellow Israelites.

accursed.etymology: From Middle English *acursed*, from *acursen* (“to curse”), from Old English *ācursian*, from *ā-* + *cursian*, from *curs* (“curse”).

senses.definition: The person charged with an offense; the defendant in a criminal case.
Having been accused; being the target of accusations.
senses.example: The accused man sat quietly while the jury listened to the prosecution's opening statement.

core.definition: The person formally charged with a crime or offense and facing trial, also called the defendant in court.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable. The ending -ed is pronounced as /d/ after the z sound, so it does not form a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal and news writing; it describes a charged person and does not imply guilt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the accused in legal writing, news reports, and courtroom discussions, especially in phrases like the rights of the accused. In a trial, judges and lawyers more often say the defendant, but news writing uses the accused before and during trials. Saying the accused says he was at home is a normal sentence in an American news story.

distinctions.note: Defendant is the standard legal term in court, while the accused is more common in news and general legal writing, especially for criminal cases.
A suspect is someone police are investigating but who has not yet been formally charged, while the accused has been charged.

examples.everyday: The news said the accused was a neighbor of mine, and I could not believe it.
examples.professional: The legal team must provide the accused with the discovery documents before the hearing next month.
examples.analytical: A fair legal system protects the accused by presuming innocence until guilt is proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

nuance.analogy: The accused is like a person in the spotlight: charged and under scrutiny, but not yet proven guilty.
nuance.etymology: From accuse, from Latin accusare 'to call to account', from ad- 'to' plus causa 'cause, lawsuit'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable, as in uh-KYOO-zed; the word has two syllables.
Using the accused to mean guilty; in American legal culture the accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

senses.definition: Having the power or quality of acting; causing change; communicating action or motion; acting;—opposed to passive, that receives.
senses.example: certain active principles

senses.definition: Quick in physical movement; of an agile and vigorous body; nimble.
senses.example: an active child or animal

senses.definition: In action; actually proceeding; working; in force.
senses.example: active laws

senses.definition: Emitting hot materials, such as lava, smoke, or steam, or producing tremors.
senses.example: The volcano remained active, with steam rising from its crater and small tremors every night.

senses.definition: Given to action; constantly engaged in action; energetic; diligent; busy.
senses.example: an active man of business

senses.definition: Requiring or implying action or exertion.
senses.example: active employment or service

senses.definition: Given to action rather than contemplation; practical; operative.
senses.example: an active rather than a speculative statesman

senses.definition: Brisk; lively.
senses.example: an active demand for corn

senses.definition: Implying or producing rapid action.
senses.example: an active disease

senses.definition: About verbs.
senses.example: The grammar lesson explained which sentences use active verbs and which use passive ones.

senses.definition: Applied to a form of the verb; — opposed to passive. See active voice.
senses.example: Rewrite the sentence in the active voice so the subject clearly performs the action.

senses.definition: Applied to verbs which assert that the subject acts upon or affects something else; transitive.
senses.example: The verb 'break' is active when it takes an object, as in 'She broke the vase.'

senses.definition: Applied to all verbs that express action as distinct from mere existence or state.
senses.example: Unlike 'be' or 'seem,' the verb 'run' is active because it describes an action.

senses.definition: Eligible to be processed by a compiler or interpreter.
senses.example: Only the files marked active are processed by the compiler during the nightly build.

senses.definition: Not passive.
Enjoying a role in anal sex in which he penetrates, rather than being penetrated by his partner.
A person or thing that is acting or capable of acting.
senses.example: In the formula, the active is the ingredient that actually does the work.

senses.definition: Any component that is not passive. See Passivity (engineering).
senses.example: The engineers modeled the circuit's active components separately from its passive resistors and capacitors.

core.definition: Doing things and taking part in something; not idle, passive, or sitting still.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the i is short, not like 'eye'. The final v is voiced, so do not turn the ending into 'AK-teef'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive, suggesting energy and engagement. Neutral in grammar and technical uses such as 'active ingredient'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'active' for people who exercise, volunteer, or stay involved, as in 'She's very active in her church.' The natural pattern is 'active in' plus a noun. In casual talk, 'Are you active?' often means 'Do you exercise?' The adverb 'actively' is more common in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Busy means your time is full of tasks; active means you are engaged and taking initiative, even when you are not overloaded.
Energetic describes high vigor or energy; active emphasizes taking part or moving, which may or may not involve high energy.

examples.everyday: My grandmother is still very active, and she walks to the farmers market every Saturday.
examples.professional: Please be active in the sprint review so we can catch problems before the release.
examples.analytical: A reasoning agent must be active rather than passive, forming hypotheses instead of only absorbing data.

nuance.analogy: Like an engine that is running, not a parked car with the keys in it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin activus, from agere, 'to drive, do'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'active to my job' instead of 'active in my job' or 'committed to my job'.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long e ('AK-teev') instead of the short i.

active.etymology: From Middle English *actyf*, from Old French *actif*, from Latin *activus*, from *ago* (“to do, to act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **h₂éǵeti*.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of argumentum ad hominem: A fallacious objection to an argument or factual claim by appealing to a characteristic or belief of the person making the argument or claim, rather than by addressing the substance of the argument or producing evidence against the claim; an attempt to argue against an opponent's idea by discrediting the opponent themselves.
A personal attack.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Of or relating to this kind of fallacious objection.
senses.example: Well that's an ad hominem argument.

senses.definition: In an ad hominem manner.
senses.example: He tried to make his case by arguing ad hominem.

core.definition: An attack on the person making an argument, rather than on the argument itself, used to dismiss the argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HAH in the second word, and keep the last two syllables weak. Don't pronounce the final -em as a strong 'em'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It labels a rhetorical foul and implies the speaker is avoiding the real issue.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ad hominem in debates, classrooms, politics and online arguments, as in 'that's just ad hominem.' Usually it's written as two words, ad hominem, though the hyphen appears too. Calling a remark ad hominem is a polite way to say someone attacked the person rather than the point.

distinctions.note: A personal attack is any insult; it becomes ad hominem only when it is used to dismiss someone's argument.
An ad hominem attacks the person; a straw man misrepresents the argument itself.

examples.everyday: When my brother said my idea was wrong because I'm always late, that was pure ad hominem.
examples.professional: Your comment about the author's background is ad hominem; please respond to the methodology instead.
examples.analytical: Dismissing the study because its funder has an interest is ad hominem unless the conflict actually invalidates the data.

nuance.analogy: Like arguing that a recipe is bad because the cook is clumsy.
nuance.etymology: Latin, 'to the person': ad, 'to' + hominem, accusative of homo, 'human being'.
common_mistakes: Calling any insult ad hominem; it is only a fallacy when used to dismiss the argument.
Using the hyphenated form as a noun in formal writing; the two-word form is more standard.
patterns: (also adj.) an ad hominem attack (on sb)

ad-hominem.etymology: Ellipsis of the Latin expression *argumentum ad hominem* (“argument at the person”).

senses.definition: The act of adducing or bringing forward.
The action by which the parts of the body are drawn towards its axis.
senses.example: Physical therapy for her hip focused on strengthening the muscles responsible for adduction.

core.definition: The act of bringing forward evidence, a reason, or an example to support a claim.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, DUK, and pronounce the final syllable as 'shun' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term from argument and logic, with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, adduction appears mostly in formal writing and in anatomy, where it means the movement of a body part toward the midline of the body. The argument sense is rare and mostly academic, so most Americans would use 'evidence' or 'citation' in ordinary speech. In a medical context, you may hear the anatomical sense instead, so check the setting.

distinctions.note: Abduction means kidnapping or, in logic, inference to the best explanation, while adduction means bringing forward evidence or moving a limb toward the body.
Evidence is the everyday word for facts that support a claim, while adduction names the act of bringing that evidence forward in a formal argument.

examples.everyday: The lawyer's adduction of old receipts was what finally convinced the judge.
examples.professional: The report's adduction of customer complaints makes the case for fixing the checkout flow.
examples.analytical: Her adduction of historical sources supports the thesis, though the argument depends on how she reads them.

nuance.analogy: Adduction is like a lawyer laying exhibits on the table, one by one, until the jury can see the whole case.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adductio, 'a bringing to,' from adducere, 'to lead to.'
common_mistakes: Using the provided IPA stress pattern, which places stress on the first syllable and is wrong for this word.
Confusing adduction with abduction, which is a very different word.

adduction.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *adductio*, from *adducō* (“to bring to oneself”), from *ad* + *ducō* (“to lead”).

senses.definition: The act of admonishing.
senses.example: Her quiet admonishment of the team after the missed deadline made everyone rethink their priorities.

core.definition: A stern warning or scolding about someone's bad behavior or mistake.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAHN, the second syllable, and the first vowel is a reduced schwa. The final syllable is weak, so 'ment' is said quickly as 'munt.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a stern rebuke, though it can be mild in context.
nuance.usage_note: Admonishment is less common than admonition and mostly appears in formal writing or older texts. In conversation, Americans say 'a warning,' 'a talking-to,' or 'a reprimand.' In careful writing, admonition is the standard noun.

distinctions.note: Admonition is the preferred noun in careful writing and religious contexts; admonishment is a less common synonym with the same meaning.
A reprimand is a formal, often official rebuke; admonishment can be informal and gentler.
A warning focuses on future danger; admonishment focuses on criticizing a past action.

examples.everyday: My coach gave me a quick admonishment for being late to practice again.
examples.professional: HR sent a written admonishment after the third missed deadline, which is standard before a formal review.
examples.analytical: The text's repeated admonishments function less as punishment than as a call to renewed moral attention.

nuance.etymology: Formed from admonish plus the suffix -ment, meaning the act or result of admonishing.
common_mistakes: Using admonishment when admonition is the more standard noun
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'AD-mon-ish-ment'

senses.definition: A form of Christianity which maintains that Jesus is divine only in the sense that God the Father adopted him, either at Jesus' birth, or at his death, as opposed to the orthodox understanding of the nature of the Trinity.
senses.example: Early church councils rejected adoptionism because it made Jesus divine only by adoption.

core.definition: The early Christian heresy that Jesus was merely a man whom God adopted as his son, rather than eternally divine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DAHP, the second syllable. The -ism ending is a reduced 'iz-um', with the -tion ending pronounced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in theological use, since it names a condemned heresy; neutral in historical description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'adoptionism' almost exclusively in academic theology, church history, or seminary discussions. It is not a casual word. In a conversation about faith, a speaker would normally explain it briefly, since many listeners would not know it. Some scholars also use it for the Spanish controversy of the eighth century.

distinctions.note: Arianism held that the Son was created and subordinate to the Father, while adoptionism held that Jesus became God's son at a point in time, through adoption.
Modalism claimed the Father, Son, and Spirit are successive modes of one person, while adoptionism claimed that Jesus was a human who later became divine by adoption.

examples.everyday: My friend said he had read about adoptionism, the old idea that Jesus only became God's son later on.
examples.professional: Our seminary reading group traced adoptionism from Paul of Samosata to the Spanish debates of the eighth century.
examples.analytical: Adoptionism treats Jesus' divine sonship as a status conferred on a human, which Nicene theology rejected by affirming the eternal generation of the Son from the Father.

nuance.analogy: Adoptionism is like saying a man became a king by being crowned later, rather than being born into the royal line from the beginning.
nuance.etymology: From adoption, from Latin adoptare, plus the suffix -ism, a term coined in theological writing.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'adoption' in everyday sense, which is a legal act of taking in a child.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'AD-op-shun-ism'; the main stress is on DAHP.
nuance.biblical_note: Adoptionists read certain texts as showing Jesus becoming Son of God at a particular moment. Romans 1:4 says Jesus was declared to be Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead, which adoptionists used to argue for a conferred status. Luke 3:22 describes the voice at Jesus' baptism calling him beloved Son, which some read as the moment of adoption. The orthodox reply is that these passages declare or reveal a sonship that was already his in eternity.

senses.definition: One who believes in or supports adoptionism.
(uncommon) One who supports adoption.
senses.example: As an adoptionist, she spoke at town halls about foster care reform and easier paperwork.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to adoptionism.
senses.example: Historians debate whether the adoptionist controversy shaped later Christian creeds about Christ.

core.definition: A person who holds adoptionism, the belief that Jesus became God's Son through adoption rather than eternal begetting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DAHP, and -tion is pronounced shun, so the middle sound is /ʃən/, not tee-on. Learners often stress the ending, as in ad-op-shuh-NIST; keep the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative or accusatory in most church settings, since adoptionism was condemned as a heresy; neutral in academic history of doctrine.
nuance.usage_note: Adoptionist is almost entirely a term from theology and church history, and Americans use it mainly in seminaries, university courses, and doctrinal debates. Calling someone an adoptionist in a church setting is an accusation of heresy, so use it carefully. Outside theology, the dictionary sense 'one who supports adoption' is uncommon; say 'an advocate for adoption' instead.

distinctions.note: Arians held that the Son was created and subordinate to the Father, while adoptionists held that the human Jesus was adopted as Son at baptism or resurrection.
Modalists said one God appears in different modes, while adoptionists said a human being became the Son by adoption.

examples.everyday: My pastor said some early Christians were adoptionists, who thought Jesus only became God's Son at his baptism.
examples.professional: In my seminar paper I argue that the Spanish adoptionist controversy shaped how Carolingian theologians defined Christ's sonship.
examples.analytical: Adoptionist Christology must explain how a human adopted at baptism could share the divine nature without reducing the Son to a creature.

nuance.analogy: An adoptionist is like someone who says a lamp only becomes a light when first switched on, rather than being light from its origin.
nuance.etymology: From adoption, from Latin adoptio, plus the suffix -ist for one who holds a belief.
common_mistakes: Using adoptionist to mean someone who supports adoption; in theology it names a heresy, so the meaning is very different.
Stressing the ending, as in uh-dahp-shuh-NIST; the stress stays on DAHP.
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself is not in Scripture, but adoptionists appealed to passages that speak of God's Son being declared or recognized at a moment in time. Mark 1:11 records the heavenly voice at Jesus' baptism, which adoptionists read as the moment of adoption. Romans 1:4 says Jesus was declared Son of God in power by his resurrection, which they also cited. Psalm 2:7 speaks of the Lord's decree to the king as son, a text used in the same debate. Orthodox Christians read these as public manifestations of the Son's eternal sonship rather than its beginning.

senses.definition: To make more beautiful and attractive; to decorate.
senses.example: a man adorned with noble statuary and columns

core.definition: To make something more beautiful by adding decorations or ornaments to it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, which is a single strong vowel, and the r is pronounced clearly in American English. The final n is syllabic and does not need an extra vowel; avoid saying 'uh-DOR-nuh.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests tasteful, pleasing decoration, and it works in both literal and figurative contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'adorn' mostly in writing, in formal descriptions, or in speech that sounds deliberately elevated, such as a wedding speech or a magazine article. In everyday conversation, people say 'decorate' instead. You might hear 'adorned with' in a description of a dress or a room, which sounds natural and polished.

distinctions.note: Decorate is the everyday word for adding things to make a space or object look nice; adorn sounds more formal and suggests the decoration is attractive in itself.
Embellish means adding extra detail, often to a story or account, so it can imply exaggeration; adorn does not carry that sense.

examples.everyday: My sister always adorns her cakes with fresh flowers, so they look like something from a bakery.
examples.professional: Before the launch, the designers wanted to adorn the dashboard with color, but the accessibility review asked them to keep the layout simple.
examples.analytical: The medieval manuscript is adorned with miniatures that serve not only to decorate the text but to interpret it.

nuance.analogy: To adorn something is like putting a frame around a painting: the frame does not change the painting's content, but it makes the whole thing look more finished and attractive.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adornare 'to equip, furnish, decorate,' from ad- 'to' plus ornare 'to equip, adorn.'
common_mistakes: Using 'adorn' for a practical addition, such as putting a new handle on a door; 'decorate' or 'add' is more natural.
Forgetting that the thing decorated is the direct object, as in 'adorn the room,' not 'adorn with the room.'
Mispronouncing the final n as 'adorn-ed' with an extra syllable in the base form.

adorn.etymology: From Middle English *adornen*, *adournen*, from Latin *adōrnō*; from *ad-* + *ōrnō*.

senses.definition: One who enjoys adventures.
senses.example: My grandfather was an adventurer who loved sailing, hiking, and exploring unknown places.

senses.definition: A person who seeks a fortune in new and possibly risky (physically dangerous or financially risky) enterprises.
senses.example: Gold fever drew many adventurers to the rivers of California in 1849.

senses.definition: A soldier of fortune.
senses.example: The old adventurer had fought in three wars for whoever paid him best.

senses.definition: A speculator.
senses.example: The bank collapsed after reckless adventurers bet heavily on unregulated mortgage securities.

senses.definition: A person who tries to advance their social position by somewhat devious means.
senses.example: The duke's new son-in-law was an adventurer who had charmed his way into high society.

senses.definition: A player of adventure games or text adventures.
senses.example: Our team's best adventurer solved the puzzle in under an hour, saving everyone's evening.

core.definition: A person who seeks risky, exciting experiences, or who pursues wealth or fame through bold, uncertain ventures.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VEN, the second syllable. The last two syllables are both r-colored and unstressed, so do not add an extra 'ay' sound before the final -er.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually suggests bravery and curiosity, though in some contexts it can suggest someone reckless or opportunistic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adventurer for people who like to travel, climb or explore, and sometimes for someone chasing money in risky schemes. Calling someone 'an adventurer' is usually a compliment, but 'fortune hunter' or 'opportunist' carries a more negative tone. In casual talk, people often say 'she's always up for an adventure' instead.

distinctions.note: An explorer seeks to discover unknown places for knowledge, while an adventurer seeks thrill or personal gain.
Risk-taker is a general term for anyone who accepts risk, while adventurer implies a quest or an exciting undertaking.
A fortune hunter specifically seeks money, often through a marriage or quick gain, and usually sounds negative.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a real adventurer; he has already kayaked the Colorado twice.
examples.professional: She is a bit of an adventurer, always willing to take on the riskiest pilot project.
examples.analytical: The Romantic figure of the adventurer, from Byron's wanderers to the modern traveler, defines the self by movement rather than home.

nuance.analogy: An adventurer is like a sailor who would rather face open water than stay in the safe harbor.
nuance.etymology: From adventure plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using adventurer as an adjective, as in 'he is adventurer'; the adjective is adventurous.
Adding an extra syllable, saying 'adventure-er' with a full vowel on the last part.

senses.definition: The process by which the price and quantity of goods or services in a given market is altered due to one party having information that the other party cannot have at reasonable cost.
senses.example: It is adverse selection that leads US workers who anticipate high family medical expenditure to seek employers with superior health insurance coverage for their employees.

core.definition: In economics and insurance, a market problem where one side's private information leads the other side to pick the wrong deals, often the riskiest buyers.

pronunciation.tip: Put the strongest stress on AD in adverse, then on LEK in selection; the -verse part is r-colored with no vowel after it. Learners often stress SELECT-ion or add an extra syllable to -tion, which is pronounced shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the term describes a market failure, so it carries a negative sense about outcomes but no judgment of people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mainly in economics, finance, insurance and policy discussions. You will hear it in health insurance debates, where people who expect high medical costs are more likely to buy coverage. It is not used in casual conversation, where you would say the insurance pool got worse.

distinctions.note: Adverse selection happens before a contract, when one party hides its risk; moral hazard happens after the contract, when a protected party takes more risk.
Asymmetric information is the broader condition of unequal knowledge; adverse selection is one market result of that condition.

examples.everyday: My friend said the insurance company asks so many health questions because of adverse selection, since sick people sign up more often.
examples.professional: Our pricing model has to account for adverse selection, because customers who expect large claims are more likely to buy the policy.
examples.analytical: Akerlof's lemons argument shows that adverse selection can drive high-quality goods out of a market when buyers cannot tell quality apart.

nuance.analogy: Like a used-car lot where the owners who most want to sell are the ones who know the car is a lemon.
nuance.etymology: Adverse comes from Latin adversus 'turned against'; selection comes from Latin selectio 'a choosing out'.
common_mistakes: Using the plural adverse selections; the concept is normally uncountable.
Confusing it with moral hazard, which happens after the contract is signed.
Stressing SELECT-ion instead of suh-LEK-shun.

core.definition: A king of the Amalekites in the Old Testament, whom King Saul spared against God's command and whom the prophet Samuel put to death.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AY, and say the second syllable as 'gag,' with a short 'a' sound. The name rhymes with 'bag' in the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary usage, but in biblical contexts it signals a dangerous enemy of Israel and the story of disobedience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'Agag' outside Bible study, sermons or religious conversation. You may hear it in phrases like 'Samuel hewed Agag in pieces,' which people say when discussing obedience. Outside church, most people would not know the name without explanation.

distinctions.note: Amalek is the name of the people or ancestor, while Agag is the king of the Amalekites in 1 Samuel 15.
Haman is called the Agagite in the book of Esther, which links him to Agag as a descendant or kinsman in later Jewish tradition.

examples.everyday: At church we heard the story of Saul sparing Agag, and it made everyone think about obeying God fully.
examples.professional: In our leadership training, we used the story of Agag as a case study in incomplete obedience.
examples.analytical: Samuel's words to Saul in 1 Samuel 15 make Agag a symbol of the cost of partial obedience to God's command.

nuance.analogy: Agag is like a warning sign on a road: his story shows what happens when a command is only partly obeyed.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew personal name 'Agag (אֲגַג), of uncertain meaning, used as a royal title or name for Amalekite kings.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'AH-gag' with an open 'a' like the 'a' in 'father'; the vowel is closer to 'ay.'
Confusing Agag with Amalek, the people or the earlier ancestor, when Agag is the king.
nuance.biblical_note: Agag was the king of the Amalekites, enemies of Israel, whom God ordered Saul to destroy completely. Numbers 24:7 mentions Agag in Balaam's oracle, saying that Israel's king will be higher than Agag. 1 Samuel 15 tells how Saul spared Agag and the best of the livestock, and Samuel declared that obedience is better than sacrifice. In 1 Samuel 15:33 Samuel put Agag to death before the LORD. The book of Esther later calls Haman the Agagite, linking him to this royal enemy.

senses.definition: Aggravation; bother.
senses.example: Don't start aggro with the neighbors over a parking space.

senses.definition: Aggressive behavior; loud, intimidating behavior that convincingly threatens violence without necessarily actually becoming violent.
senses.example: Move along, lads; we don't want any aggro.

senses.definition: A measure of how belligerent a player is – a high value may inspire either avoidance or preemptive hostile action from enemies.
senses.example: The tank's aggro was high enough that the goblins ignored everyone else in the party.

senses.definition: (MMORPG slang) Hostile attention from an enemy that should target players with better defenses.
senses.example: The healer pulled aggro from the boss, and now the whole raid is in trouble.

senses.definition: (MMORPG slang) To become aggressive towards the player's character.
senses.example: Do they aggro on sight or sound?

senses.definition: (MMORPG slang) Liable to attack without being attacked first (said of monsters).
senses.example: The skeletons in the crypt are aggro, so don't walk in without a shield.

senses.definition: Hardcore, aggressive.
senses.example: That new shooter is aggro, with fast rounds and no hand-holding at all.

core.definition: Hostile, confrontational behavior, or trouble and hassle from someone who is looking for a fight or an argument (informal slang).

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the vowel in 'ag' short, like the a in 'cat'. Avoid saying 'uh-GROH', which moves the stress to the wrong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes intimidation, hassle or hostility that makes a situation unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: 'Aggro' is a clipped form of 'aggravation' that started as British slang, but Americans use it, especially among young people, skaters, sports fans and gamers. In ordinary American English, people more often say 'trouble', 'a hassle' or 'a hard time', so use 'aggro' only in relaxed conversation. Phrases such as 'give someone aggro' and 'get aggro' are informal and can sound rough.

distinctions.note: Aggravation is the standard word for annoyance or irritation, while aggro is informal and suggests active hostility or confrontation.
A hassle is a minor, tiring nuisance, but aggro implies that someone is being openly hostile or intimidating.
A beef is a grudge or long-standing complaint, while aggro is the aggressive behavior or conflict that comes from it.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor gave me aggro about the trash cans, so I just moved them and let it go.
examples.professional: The vendor kept giving us aggro over the invoice, so I looped in procurement to settle it.
examples.analytical: Sociologists of youth culture describe aggro as a performed display of toughness that signals a willingness to fight without necessarily fighting.

nuance.analogy: Like the tension in the air before a thunderstorm, aggro is the feeling that a fight could break out at any moment.
nuance.etymology: Clipped from aggravation; the slang form arose in British English.
common_mistakes: Using 'aggro' in formal writing, where 'aggravation' or 'conflict' is expected.
Pronouncing it 'uh-GROH' with stress on the second syllable.

senses.definition: The study of moral questions raised by AI, such as fairness, privacy and accountability.
senses.example: Our graduate seminar spent a week on AI ethics, debating fairness and consent in models.

core.definition: The study of moral questions raised by AI, such as fairness, privacy, transparency and accountability.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters A and I with stress on the I. In ethics the stress is on the first syllable, the th is voiceless as in thin, and the ending is a short iks.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals responsibility and care, though some people hear it as vague if no concrete rules follow.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use AI ethics as a field of study, a team name or a set of company principles. You might hear it in university courses, tech company reports or policy debates. In casual conversation people more often say 'responsible AI' or 'AI bias'. A natural reply is 'Yes, that's a big issue right now.'

distinctions.note: AI safety focuses on preventing dangerous technical failures and misuse, while AI ethics focuses on fairness, rights and social impact.
AI ethics asks what is right, while AI governance defines the rules, roles and processes that turn ethical principles into practice.

examples.everyday: My sister teaches a class on AI ethics at her community college.
examples.professional: Before we launch the hiring model, the AI ethics review needs to check whether it disadvantages any group of applicants.
examples.analytical: AI ethics cannot simply import human moral categories, because algorithmic systems distribute responsibility across developers, data and deployers in new ways.

nuance.analogy: It works like a building code for the moral side of AI, asking what should be allowed, not only what can be built.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ēthikos, meaning relating to character or habit, from ēthos.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing ethics as 'eth-eeks' with a long final vowel; the ending is short.
Confusing ethics with ethnics, which has a different meaning and pronunciation.

conversation.text: AI ethics examines the moral questions raised by AI, such as fairness, privacy, and responsibility.
Our AI ethics board reviews any project that uses biometric data.
A course on AI ethics is now required for every data scientist on the team.

senses.definition: Without aim, purpose, or direction.
senses.example: an aimless life

core.definition: Without a clear purpose, direction or goal; wandering or acting with no sense of where one is going.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AYM. The final -less is pronounced with a reduced vowel, like 'lus,' not 'lis' or 'less.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly critical; it suggests a lack of focus, purpose or energy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aimless to describe people who seem lost, wandering or unmotivated, as well as conversations, plans or actions with no clear point. It can be sympathetic when describing a person going through a hard time, but it is often a mild criticism. Use 'aimless' for direction and 'pointless' for activities that have no value.

distinctions.note: Pointless means having no useful result or value, while aimless means lacking direction or purpose.
Directionless is close in meaning but more descriptive of a state of confusion, while aimless often describes motion or behavior.

examples.everyday: After he graduated, he spent months drifting around the country in an aimless way, not sure what he wanted.
examples.professional: The project felt aimless because nobody had defined success, so the team kept adding features without a clear plan.
examples.analytical: The novel portrays modern youth as aimless, though the author suggests this condition reflects economic and social dislocation.

nuance.analogy: An aimless walk is like a boat without a rudder: it moves, but it has no course and goes wherever the current takes it.
nuance.etymology: From aim (noun) plus the suffix -less, meaning 'without.'
common_mistakes: Using 'aimless' as an adverb; the adverb form is 'aimlessly.'
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'less' sound rather than a reduced vowel.

senses.definition: An airfield (an area designated for the takeoff and landing of aircraft), including one or more runways and (for commercial airports) one or more passenger terminals.
senses.example: She met Sam and the others at the airport at 7:00 am.

core.definition: A place with runways and terminals where airplanes take off, land, and load passengers and cargo.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AIR. The 'r' in both syllables is clear in American English, and the second vowel is the 'or' sound in 'port', which is often merged with 'caught' and 'pot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can carry stress or excitement, depending on whether the speaker is traveling or picking someone up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use airport in everyday speech, travel plans, and business travel, for example 'I'm heading to the airport at six.' In casual talk, people often say 'the airport' even when they mean a specific terminal. A natural reply is 'Which terminal are you flying out of?'

distinctions.note: An airfield is a flat area for aircraft, and it may not have passenger terminals, while an airport usually serves commercial passengers.
An air terminal usually means the passenger building or check-in facility, while airport refers to the whole facility.

collocations: drop someone off at the airport
catch a flight at the airport
pick someone up from the airport

examples.everyday: Can you pick me up at the airport on Friday? My flight lands around noon.
examples.professional: Our sales team flies out of the airport at six tomorrow, so let's finish the slides before they leave.
examples.analytical: The airport operates as a node in a larger transport network, where delays in one terminal can ripple across cities and supply chains.

nuance.analogy: An airport is like a bus station for airplanes: it is where planes stop, load, and depart on schedule.
nuance.etymology: Air comes from Latin aer; port comes from Latin portus, 'harbor' or 'gate'.
common_mistakes: Omitting the article, as in 'I am going to airport'; American English says 'I am going to the airport'.
Using 'on the airport' instead of 'at the airport' for a location.

conversation.text: How early should I get to the airport for an international flight?
I'll pick you up at the airport; just text me when you land.
The airport is about thirty minutes from downtown without traffic.

senses.definition: The quality of being airtight.

core.definition: The quality of being sealed so tightly that air cannot get in or out, as in windows, containers, or buildings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AIR, and the t in tight is often clear before the n, though it can be lightly reduced in fast speech. The final syllable is short and reduced, so say 'nus.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical measure, though it can be positive when it means good sealing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use airtightness in building inspections, energy efficiency discussions, packaging, and food storage. In everyday talk, people more often use the adjective airtight, as in 'a airtight container.' The noun is most useful when you are discussing a measurable quality.

distinctions.note: Sealing is the action or method of closing a gap, while airtightness is the quality of the result.
Watertightness refers to keeping water out, while airtightness refers to keeping air out, and the two can differ in a building or container.
Hermeticity is a formal technical term for a completely sealed system, while airtightness is the everyday technical word.

examples.everyday: Those old windows let in drafts all winter, so the airtightness is pretty bad.
examples.professional: The inspector measured the airtightness of the building envelope before approving the permit.
examples.analytical: The airtightness of a sealed jar preserves its contents, yet the same seal can trap gas and build dangerous pressure.

nuance.analogy: Like a zipper pressed shut with no gap along its edges.
nuance.etymology: From airtight, meaning air plus tight, with the noun ending -ness.
common_mistakes: Writing it with extra hyphens, as in air-tight-ness, instead of airtightness.
Using airtightness as a verb-like action, when people usually say seal or seal off.

senses.definition: In addition; besides; as well; further; too.
senses.example: Everyone had eggs for breakfast, but Alice also had toast. Also, she finished hers in under half an hour.

senses.definition: And in addition.
senses.example: It's a pretty dog, also loyal.

core.definition: In addition to what was just said; as well as something else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and say the 'l' clearly before the 'soh' vowel. Many Americans with the cot-caught merger say AHL-soh, which is also correct, but do not say al-so with a short 'a' as in cat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use also mainly in the middle of a sentence, before the main verb or after be, as in I also like it. At the start of a sentence, Also, is set off with a comma and sounds more formal or written. In casual speech people often say too or as well at the end of a clause.

distinctions.note: Too usually comes at the end of a clause and is more casual; also goes before the main verb and is common in writing.
Besides introduces an extra reason or point, often in an argument; also simply adds information.

examples.everyday: I'd like the iced tea, and I also want a side of fries.
examples.professional: I also need the Q3 numbers before Friday, so please send them when you can.
examples.analytical: The argument is persuasive, but it also depends on a premise the author never defends.

nuance.analogy: Also is like adding another topping to a sandwich: the original stays, and something more is added.
nuance.etymology: From Old English alswa, meaning all so or entirely so.
common_mistakes: Putting also after a main verb, as in I go also, instead of I also go.
Using also and too together, as in I also want too, which is redundant.

also.etymology: From Middle English *also*, *alswo*, *alswa* (also *als*, *as*, whence English *as*), from Old English *eallswā* (“just like, also”), from **allswā*, equivalent to *all* + *so*.

senses.definition: An individual's alternate personality or persona; another self.
senses.example: Clark Kent's coworkers finally discovered his alter ego, Superman.

senses.definition: A very close and intimate friend.

A corporation used by a person to conduct personal business in an attempt to shield himself or herself from personal liability, and which a court may penetrate by "piercing the corporate veil" to impose liability on the person when they commit fraud or injustice.
senses.example: The court pierced the veil because the owner treated the firm as his alter ego.

core.definition: A second self: an alternate personality or persona that a person shows, or a very close friend seen as another self.

pronunciation.tip: 'Alter' is a homophone of 'altar' in General American, pronounced like 'all-ter'. Stress falls on AL, and 'ego' is EE-goh, not 'EG-oh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it can describe a bold, fun persona or a close friend, but it can also suggest a hidden or darker side.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use alter ego in casual talk about a performer's stage persona, a superhero's secret identity, or a playful version of oneself, often with a light tone. In legal or business settings it has a separate technical sense. A natural reply when someone mentions a persona is 'Oh, I love that side of you,' or simply 'Tell me more about your alter ego.'

distinctions.note: A persona is the social role a person presents, while an alter ego is a more distinct second self, often a separate identity.
A doppelgänger is a double who looks like you, while an alter ego is a different personality or identity.

examples.everyday: At karaoke, my cousin becomes her alter ego, a flamboyant rock singer who never shows up at family dinners.
examples.professional: The client's internal dashboard is basically the alter ego of the public report, showing all the numbers we leave out.
examples.analytical: Jung's notion of the persona describes the social mask, while the alter ego points to a more radical split within the self.

nuance.analogy: Like a stage name for the self: the same person in a costume that unlocks different powers.
nuance.etymology: From Latin alter, 'the other', and ego, 'I'.
common_mistakes: Writing altar ego, which confuses it with the church altar.
Pronouncing ego as EG-oh, when the standard American pronunciation is EE-goh.

senses.definition: To fill (someone) with surprise and wonder; to astonish, to astound, to surprise.
senses.example: He was amazed when he found that the girl was a robot.

senses.definition: Fear, terror.
senses.example: The knight trembled with amaze as the dragon rose from the lake.

senses.definition: (poetic) Amazement, astonishment; an instance of this.
senses.example: To her amaze, the old oak had survived the storm without losing a single branch.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: Clipping of amazing.
senses.example: That concert was totally amaze, honestly the best night all year.

core.definition: To fill someone with great surprise or wonder; to astonish them, often in a positive way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MAYZ. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, so do not say 'AH-mayz'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It usually suggests admiration or wonder, though it can express shock.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say 'You amaze me' or 'I'm amazed' when praising someone or reacting to something impressive. It is stronger than 'surprise' and sounds warm rather than neutral. In casual talk, people often say 'That blows my mind' or 'I can't believe it' instead.

distinctions.note: Surprise is any unexpected event; amaze is stronger and usually carries a sense of wonder or admiration.
The two are close in meaning, but astonish is more formal and suggests greater shock.

examples.everyday: You ran the whole marathon with no training? You really amaze me.
examples.professional: Your team cut the query time in half in one sprint, and that amazed the whole leadership group.
examples.analytical: Scripture often pictures people amazed at God's works, and that response raises the question of what proper wonder should lead us to do.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden sunrise over a dark field, amaze lights up the mind all at once.
nuance.etymology: Middle English amasen, from Old English āmasian 'to stupefy, bewilder'.
common_mistakes: Using 'amazed of' instead of 'amazed by' or 'amazed at'
Saying 'I am amazing' to describe your own feeling; 'amazing' describes the thing that causes the feeling, while 'amazed' describes the person feeling it
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, the Greek verb existemi, 'to be beside oneself, astonished', is used for the crowds' reaction to wonders (Acts 2:7 reports that the crowds in Jerusalem were amazed to hear Galileans speaking in their own languages). Luke 2:47 describes those who heard the boy Jesus in the temple as amazed at his understanding and his answers. Mark 5:42 describes people overcome with amazement when Jairus's daughter was restored, using the Greek noun ekstasis.

amaze.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *amased* (“to bewilder, perplex”) (attested chiefly in the past participle form, and thus often difficult to distinguish from *amased*), from Old English *āmasian* (“to confuse, astonish”), from *ā-* + **masian* (“to…

senses.definition: Formerly thought to be the product of a plant.

A hard, generally yellow to brown translucent or transparent fossil resin from extinct coniferous trees of the pine genus, used for jewelry, decoration and later dissolved as a binder in varnishes. One variety, blue amber, appears blue rather than yellow under direct sunlight.
A yellow-orange color.
senses.example: amber:

senses.definition: Hesitance to proceed, or limited approval to proceed; an amber light.
The stop codon (nucleotide triplet) "UAG", or a mutant which has this stop codon at a premature place in its DNA sequence.
senses.example: an amber codon, an amber mutation, an amber suppressor

senses.definition: Of a brownish yellow color, like that of most amber.
To perfume or flavor with ambergris.
senses.example: ambered wine, an ambered room

senses.definition: To take on the yellow color of amber.
(rare) To preserve in amber.
senses.example: an ambered fly
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare, poetic) To cause to take on the yellow color of amber.
senses.label: rare, poetic

core.definition: A hard, yellowish-brown fossil tree resin, used for jewelry; also the warm yellow-orange color of this resin.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the r clear and don't stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warmth, beauty, and preciousness, and it is often used for natural or glowing objects.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'amber' is the common name for the yellow light on a traffic signal, which means slow down, and it appears in 'Amber Alert', the emergency system for child abductions. For the color, Americans often describe things as 'amber-colored' or 'the color of honey'. The word is used in everyday speech, especially when talking about drinks or jewelry.

distinctions.note: Golden is a brighter, more general yellow; amber is deeper and more brownish-orange.
Ochre is a dull earthy yellow-brown pigment, while amber is translucent and glowing.

examples.everyday: The light turned amber, so I slowed down and waited for it to change.
examples.professional: The traffic-signal project flags any amber phase that lasts under three seconds as a safety risk.
examples.analytical: The paleontologist argued that an insect preserved in amber gives a snapshot of a forest that no longer exists.

nuance.analogy: Like honey that has hardened and kept the moment it was made inside it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English ambre, from Arabic ʿanbar, 'ambergris', which was later applied to the fossil resin.
common_mistakes: Thinking amber is a mineral or gemstone; it is fossilized tree resin.
Using 'amber' to mean only the color of a traffic light instead of the color in general.

amber.etymology: From Middle English *ambre*, *aumbre*, from Old French *aumbre*, *ambre*, from Arabic *عَنْبَر* (“ambergris”), from *𐭠𐭭𐭡𐭫* (“ambergris”).

senses.definition: The total, aggregate or sum of material.
senses.example: The amount of atmospheric pollution threatens a health crisis.

senses.definition: A quantity or volume.
senses.example: Pour a small amount of water into the dish.

senses.definition: To total or evaluate.
senses.example: The money in my pocket amounts to three dollars and change.

senses.definition: To be the tantamount to; to reach up to the level of.
senses.example: He was a pretty good student, but never amounted to much professionally.

core.definition: A quantity or total of something, especially a measurable or countable sum of money, time, or material.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, MOWNT, with the diphthong 'ow' as in 'house'. Many learners say 'AM-ount' with stress on the first syllable, which is wrong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word itself carries no positive or negative feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'amount' with uncountable nouns such as money, time, water, or sugar. For countable things, Americans say 'number' instead, as in 'a number of people' rather than 'an amount of people'. In shopping and cooking the word comes up constantly, such as 'How much of this do I need?' or 'the right amount of salt'.

distinctions.note: Number is used for countable items, while amount is used for things you measure rather than count.
Quantity is more formal or technical and is common in science, business, and inventory contexts.
Sum refers to a total of money or a calculated total of numbers, and is more specific than the general word amount.

examples.everyday: Can you add a little more milk? Just a small amount, please.
examples.professional: The total amount due on this invoice is four thousand two hundred dollars, so please check it before Friday.
examples.analytical: The amount of variance the model explains is modest, which limits how confidently we can interpret its coefficients.

nuance.analogy: Like water in a glass: you can measure how much is there without counting individual drops.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French amonter 'to mount up', from Old French amont 'upward', from a- 'to' and mont 'mountain'.
common_mistakes: Using 'an amount of people' for countable nouns; say 'a number of people' instead.
Stressing the first syllable as 'AM-ount' rather than uh-MOWNT.

amount.etymology: From Middle English *amounten* (“to mount up to, come up to, signify”), from Old French *amonter* (“to amount to”), from *amont*, *amunt* (“uphill, upward”), from the prepositional phrase *a mont* (“toward or to a mountain or heap”), from Latin *ad…

senses.definition: A right to receive amounts of money regularly over a certain fixed period, in perpetuity, or, especially, over the remaining life or lives of one or more beneficiaries.
senses.example: life annuity

core.definition: A fixed amount of money paid to a person at regular intervals, usually yearly, often for life or for a set number of years, typically bought from an insurance company.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NOO. The last syllable is a weak 'ih-tee', not a long 'ee-tee'. Americans often say the t as a soft flap, like 'tee' with a light d sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a financial term, usually used in discussions of retirement planning or insurance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use annuity mainly in personal finance and retirement planning, for example when talking about a pension alternative or an insurance product. In everyday talk people often say 'pension' for employer plans and 'retirement income' more generally. The word is often used with a qualifier such as fixed annuity or variable annuity.
word_family: annuitant (noun, a person receiving an annuity)

distinctions.note: A pension is usually an employer-provided retirement benefit, while an annuity is a contract, often bought from an insurer, that pays out regularly.
A 401(k) is a savings account for retirement that you invest in, while an annuity is a contract that pays you regular income.
Life insurance pays money to beneficiaries after death, while an annuity pays money to the owner or a beneficiary during life.

examples.everyday: My grandfather lives on an annuity he bought from his insurance company after he retired.
examples.professional: We compared the fixed annuity payouts against the company's pension options before making a recommendation.
examples.analytical: An annuity shifts longevity risk from the individual to the insurer, so its value depends heavily on mortality assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet that keeps running every month for as long as you own the contract.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin annuitas, from Latin annuus, 'yearly', from annus, 'year'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'annuity' with the stress on the first syllable instead of the second, NOO.
Confusing an annuity, which pays out, with a savings account, which holds money for you to withdraw.

annuity.etymology: From French *annuité*, from Medieval Latin *annuitās*, from Latin *annuus* (“annual”).

related: annuitant (noun, a person receiving an annuity)

senses.definition: To make or render anonymous (especially to remove personally identifying data).

core.definition: To remove or disguise personally identifying information from data or records so that the individual cannot be identified.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NAH, the second syllable, and the first syllable is a reduced uh. The ending -ize is pronounced like the word eyes with a z sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise term for a practice, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use anonymize mostly with data, survey responses, and records, as in 'we anonymized the responses.' For people it sounds formal, so in everyday talk say 'hide their names' instead. In a meeting or email it is a natural, precise word. It can sound stiff if you use it for something trivial, like a shopping list.

distinctions.note: Redact means blacking out or deleting specific text; anonymize means making whole records untraceable to a person.
Encrypt scrambles content so only key holders can read it; anonymize removes the identity link so the data cannot be traced back.

examples.everyday: I asked the app to anonymize my account before I deleted it, just to be safe.
examples.professional: Please anonymize the customer IDs before we send the file to the vendor.
examples.analytical: To anonymize a dataset properly, one must consider quasi-identifiers such as age and location, not only names.

nuance.analogy: Like peeling the labels off jars so no one can tell which jam came from which kitchen.
nuance.etymology: From anonymous, from Greek anōnymos 'without a name', plus the verb suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using anonymize only for people; it is also used for data, records, and reviews.
Saying the ending as a plain s sound, or stressing the first syllable as AH-nuh-mize.

core.definition: In Christian belief, a person or power that opposes Christ and deceives people, expected to appear before the end of the age.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AN. Say 'tee' for the middle and 'kryst' as one syllable; avoid saying 'an-TIE-christ.' British speakers sometimes say 'AN-tye,' but General American uses 'AN-tee.'

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; it names the supreme enemy of Christ, and is used figuratively for a great evil figure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Antichrist' mostly in religion, but also in popular culture, such as horror movies and political insults. It is usually capitalized when referring to the final enemy of Christ. Calling a person 'the Antichrist' is a very strong insult and often seen as offensive or exaggerated.

distinctions.note: A 'false prophet' misleads people with false teaching, while the 'Antichrist' is a specific opponent of Christ.
The 'beast' is an image in Revelation, which many readers identify with the Antichrist, but the word 'Antichrist' itself does not appear there.
'Satan' is the spiritual adversary of God, while the Antichrist is usually a human figure empowered by him.

examples.everyday: My uncle watched a movie about the Antichrist, and he said it kept him up all night.
examples.professional: In the survey, we grouped answers about the Antichrist with other end-times beliefs, such as the Rapture.
examples.analytical: John uses 'antichrist' for anyone who denies the Son, while later tradition gathered these hints into one final adversary.

nuance.analogy: A counterfeit of Christ, imitating him in order to lead people away.
nuance.etymology: From Greek antichristos, from anti- 'against, in place of' + Christos 'anointed one.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'an-TIE-christ' instead of 'AN-tee-kryst.'
Pronouncing the ch as in 'church' instead of k.
Thinking the word appears in Revelation, when it appears only in John's letters.
nuance.biblical_note: The word 'antichrist' appears only in 1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3 and 2 John 7. In 1 John 2:18, John says that antichrist is coming and that many antichrists have already appeared. In 1 John 4:3, the spirit of antichrist is the spirit that does not confess Jesus. Related figures include the 'man of lawlessness' in 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4 and the beast in Revelation 13, which many later readers connect with the Antichrist.

senses.definition: Strikingly appropriate or relevant; well suited to the circumstance or in relation to something.
Positioned at rest in respect to another, be it side-to-side, front-to-front, back-to-back, or even three-dimensionally: in apposition.
senses.example: The two panels were mounted apposite, front-to-front, so the camera could capture stereo images.

senses.definition: Related, homologous.
senses.example: The biologist identified two genes that were apposite in function across species.

senses.definition: (rare) That which is apposite; something suitable.
senses.example: Her reply was the perfect apposite to his earlier remark about trust.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Very appropriate, relevant, or well suited to a particular situation, especially in a way that is clever or striking.
